statement: Relative employment index of ages 22-25 in the most AI-exposed occupation quintile falls >= 5 pts from its 2026 level (Stanford Digital Economy Lab 'Canaries' series, last 2027 release)
status_at_phase_end: 2026 is the baseline year. Series moved from ad-hoc paper revisions to a monthly public dashboard (June 2026). The relative shortfall widened from 15% (Jul-2025 vintage) to 19% (Jun-2026 vintage), and the dashboard reported a sharpening decline (~4.4% annualised) in recent months as of Oct 2026 - momentum toward YES if sustained.

items.summary: A frontier developer's economists published a new AI-exposure measure: no systematic rise in unemployment for highly exposed workers since late 2022, but suggestive evidence that hiring of younger workers has slowed in exposed occupations.
items.detail: Massenkoff & McCrory, 'Labor market impacts of AI: A new measure and early evidence', Anthropic (Bloc A). Interested party.

items.summary: The Canaries series became a monthly public dashboard (AI Economic Indicators). First note: aggregate differences between exposed and less-exposed occupations are modest, but early-career (22-25) employment is clearly correlated with exposure; automation-type usage correlates with weaker employment, augmentation-type does not.
items.detail: Stanford Digital Economy Lab with ADP Research, launch press release and Research Note #1 (June 2026 update). Early-career workers = 7.4% of sample employment (Nov 2022).

items.summary: Revised Canaries paper (payroll data to June 2026): employment of ages 22-25 in highly AI-exposed occupations is 19% below where it would be had it kept pace with less-exposed peers, up from 15% at the July-2025 vintage. In levels, the two most-exposed quintiles fell ~11% since Nov 2022 while the three least-exposed grew ~10%. Adjustment is via reduced hiring; no comparable gap for experienced workers.
items.detail: Brynjolfsson, Chandar, Chen, 'Canaries in the Coal Mine? Six Facts...' revised 2026-08-12 (Bloc A ADP data). Authors caution: descriptive not causal; attenuates with education controls; larger than in national survey benchmarks; some pre-trends.

items.summary: In the same paper, the most-exposed quintile for ages 22-25 declined ~18 percentage points relative to the least-exposed quintile (regression estimate), the closest published figure to this indicator's quintile-level index.
items.detail: Canaries August 2026 PDF, robustness table Panel A coefficient -0.179 for ages 22-25, top vs bottom quintile (Bloc A).

items.summary: Canaries Dashboard monthly update: employment of ages 22-25 in the two most AI-exposed occupations has fallen >3% per year since Nov 2022, with the decline sharpening to ~4.4% annualised in recent months.
items.detail: Stanford Digital Economy Lab AI Economic Indicators, Canaries Dashboard update 2026-10-21, as reported by Stanford News / HAI (Oct 2026). Occupations: software developers, customer service representatives (Bloc A).

items.summary: Administrative-data studies from two small open economies outside the two blocs found no significant negative effect of AI exposure on youth or junior employment through 2025, a counterpoint to the payroll-panel pattern.
items.detail: Kauhanen & Rouvinen (2026), ETLA Working Paper 135 (Bloc T); Facius & Iacono (2026), CESifo WP 12752 (Bloc M). Exact publication dates not verified (mid-2026 approx.), cited via Alex Imas substack review.

items.summary: The Canaries series covers only Bloc A payroll data; no comparable age-by-AI-exposure employment series exists for Bloc B. The 2026 baseline level for the indicator must be fixed from the dashboard's 2026 vintages, which are revised monthly.
items.detail: Indicator uses Bloc A ADP data only; no NBS (Bloc B) equivalent series found.
